audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Tuesday, June twenty-third, twenty twenty-six. Three things are pulling focus today — Canadian higher education policy, the AI talent war, and what's happening inside eXp — and all three touch your work directly. Let's get into it.

Let's start where the most immediate business signal sits: Canadian higher education. There are three stories today that, taken together, paint a portrait of a sector under real structural stress — and that stress is your opportunity.

First and closest to home: Thompson Rivers University, your Kamloops institution, has an executive publicly warning that more budget cuts are coming — even though the university just posted an eight-point-nine million dollar operating surplus. Now, on the surface that sounds contradictory, and it is. But it's actually a very specific kind of institutional signal. When leadership can't communicate clearly about the relationship between financial results and strategic decisions, it usually means one of a few things: there's internal disagreement at the senior level, there's a longer-term structural projection that's genuinely alarming, or there's a governance problem that hasn't surfaced publicly yet. Any of those scenarios is exactly where an external strategy advisor adds clarity and credibility. TRU is right in your backyard, you understand the Kamloops context better than any outside consultant would, and this is the kind of moment where a warm, well-timed outreach can land. Worth putting on your radar as a near-term conversation.

Second, The Conversation has published a substantive analysis arguing that Canada's layered immigration restrictions — study permit caps, PGWP eligibility changes, and the general tightening posture from IRCC — are compounding into a structural deterrent for international students, not just a cyclical dip. This matters for Midya-the-consultant because it reframes the challenge for any Canadian university you might work with. The instinct inside institutions is often to treat enrolment decline as a marketing problem — better conversion funnels, stronger agent relationships, more compelling recruitment content. But if the underlying policy environment is fundamentally unfavourable, no amount of brand storytelling closes that gap. Your value as an advisor is in being honest about that distinction and helping institutions redirect effort toward the levers that actually move — domestic enrolment, graduate programming, alumni engagement, or institutional partnerships with employers. The piece is worth reading in full because it gives you the policy vocabulary to have that conversation at the right level.

Third, Minister Diab is holding a press conference today following the Forum of Ministers Responsible for Immigration — the joint federal-provincial body that coordinates immigration policy. This is one to watch in real time, because any coordinated signal from that meeting about international student pathways, whether that's a loosening or a further tightening, will immediately affect how university administrators are planning for the next intake cycle. If you have any clients or prospects in the higher-ed space, this is the briefing to follow today. The announcement could arrive by mid-afternoon.

And just to round out the higher-ed picture: University Affairs has a profile of Memorial University's new president, Janet Morrison, reflecting on her first year at the helm. It's a lighter read, but Memorial is a university that often flies under the radar in consulting conversations — it serves a specific Atlantic Canada market, it has significant research ambitions, and a new president in year one is often the most open to outside thinking. File it as a slow-burn prospect.

Now to AI, and specifically to the talent war that is reshaping the entire competitive landscape at the top of the field.

The big news: Noam Shazeer has left Google DeepMind for OpenAI. If that name doesn't immediately ring a bell, here's why it should. Shazeer is one of the eight co-authors of the two-thousand-seventeen paper 'Attention Is All You Need' — the research that introduced the Transformer architecture, which is the foundational mechanism underpinning essentially every large language model that exists today, including GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, and the tools you use in your daily work. Google paid more than two billion dollars to acqui-hire Shazeer and part of his Character.ai team. And now he's at OpenAI. That is not a routine departure. It signals two things simultaneously: first, that the researchers who genuinely believe AGI is achievable in the near term are gravitating toward OpenAI's culture and mission framing; and second, that Google, despite its enormous resources and talent base, is struggling to retain the people whose instinct is to push hardest on the frontier. For Midya-the-marketing-consultant, the downstream implication is simple: the capability gap between labs is likely to widen and shift over the next twelve to eighteen months, which means the tools you recommend to clients — and the integrations you build your consulting practice around — may look quite different by late twenty-twenty-seven. Stay close to OpenAI's product roadmap.

Separately, MIT Technology Review has a remarkable long-form piece on ASML's new EUV lithography machine — a four-hundred-million-dollar contraption the size of a double-decker bus that represents the single most critical chokepoint in global AI chip production. Every advanced semiconductor — every chip in every data centre running every AI model — must be manufactured using a machine that only ASML makes. The geopolitical dimension here is immense: the US has successfully pressured the Netherlands to restrict ASML's exports to China, which means the chip supply chain for AI infrastructure is now explicitly a tool of great-power competition. This isn't directly actionable for your consulting work, but it is the kind of systems-level context that distinguishes a senior advisor from someone who only tracks product launches. Understanding that the AI capability race is ultimately bottlenecked by a single Dutch company's machines — and that access to those machines is now a matter of national policy — helps you frame for clients why AI investment cycles are so lumpy and why capability jumps are often sudden rather than gradual.

Three marketing stories today, and they sit on a spectrum from immediately practical to strategically important.

The most consequential: Omnicom's Flywheel unit has built a tool that injects brand recommendations directly into the AI shopping assistants running on Amazon, Walmart, and Target. Think about what that means. When a consumer asks an AI assistant — whether that's Alexa, or a Walmart app chatbot, or whatever Target is running — 'what's the best laundry detergent for sensitive skin,' the answer is no longer purely algorithmic in the old SEO sense. It's now a generative output, and Flywheel has figured out how to make branded products appear favourably in those outputs. This is the applied version of everything that's been discussed theoretically about AI-driven search changing marketing. It's here, it's running at scale on the three largest retail platforms in North America, and it's being deployed by Omnicom — meaning the largest holding company in the world now has a structural advantage in retail AI placement. For your consulting practice, this is client-ready insight: if any of your prospects or clients sell through Amazon, Walmart, or Target, this conversation needs to happen now, not in a year.

On Amazon specifically: Prime Day 2026 has been shifted to a new date, and brand teams are frustrated because their planning cycles were built around the previous calendar. Adweek's piece makes a point worth extracting for your advisory work — Prime Day has now surpassed Black Friday in total transaction volume, which means it's no longer an optional activation for brands that sell online. But Amazon's unilateral ability to move the date and force brands to scramble reveals something important about platform dependency risk. This is a clean illustration for any client conversation about why diversified channel strategy isn't just a hedge against Amazon's commission rates — it's a hedge against Amazon's calendar.

And the third piece, from BBN Times, maps how digital marketing agencies are restructuring their service models around AI-altered search behaviour in twenty-twenty-six. The specifics of that article are less important than the meta-signal: agencies are publicly acknowledging that traditional SEO and paid search models are becoming obsolete. For someone positioning a consulting practice around AI in marketing, this is the ambient evidence that the market is ready. The conversation has moved from 'should we think about AI' to 'how do we restructure around AI' — and that's where consulting mandates live.

A couple of real estate items worth flagging.

On eXp: the company's newly installed COO is giving an interview centred on a single message — agents need stability in a time of change. That framing is interesting because it acknowledges, implicitly, that the instability is real. eXp has been navigating structural questions about its revenue-share model, agent retention in a slower transaction market, and the broader fallout from NAR settlement changes that have reshuffled how buyer's agent compensation works across North America. The new COO's public tone is reassuring, but the emphasis on stability usually signals that leadership knows turbulence is ongoing. For you as a property owner who's tracking eXp as an industry bellwether, keep watching for concrete operational announcements — not just messaging.

And on the macro front: US existing home sales have hit their lowest level since the Great Financial Crisis of two-thousand-eight. That is a significant data point. The American market and the Canadian market aren't perfectly correlated — we have different mortgage structures, different immigration dynamics, different supply constraints — but US demand collapse at this scale tends to ripple northward in sentiment and in cross-border capital flows. For your BC holdings specifically in Vancouver and Langley, this is context that reinforces a cautious posture on any near-term selling or buying decisions.

Locally in Kamloops, the City has released its annual financial disclosure report showing the municipal payroll has climbed to ninety million dollars. That's a notable benchmark — it's the kind of figure that will define the contours of the next budget debate, particularly as council faces pressure on infrastructure and services. No immediate action required, but it's useful context if you're following Kamloops civic matters or if TRU-related budget conversations eventually involve provincial funding dynamics.

Two global stories that deserve a moment.

Today is the ten-year anniversary of the Brexit referendum, and the timing couldn't be more pointed: Keir Starmer has resigned as UK Prime Minister less than two years after a historic Labour election win. Axios frames it well — Britain is now on its seventh prime minister since Brexit, the economy is smaller relative to peers than it was in twenty-sixteen, and the political instability that Brexit unleashed has genuinely outgrown the capacity of any single leader to contain. For you as a Canadian with international business awareness, Brexit's decade-long lesson is worth internalising: large structural disruptions — whether political, technological, or demographic — don't resolve quickly, and the initial winners of the change narrative rarely end up being the ultimate beneficiaries. That's a lens that applies to AI disruption, immigration policy, and higher-ed transformation equally.

And Oracle: the company announced twenty-one thousand job cuts, its largest ever layoff, explicitly framed as a reallocation of capital toward AI infrastructure. This continues the pattern we've seen at Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Salesforce — large enterprise tech firms are systematically converting human headcount into AI compute spend. The number that matters isn't twenty-one thousand — it's the directional certainty with which these firms are making that trade-off. They are not hedging. They believe the marginal dollar of AI investment produces more output than the marginal dollar of human labour, at least for the functions being cut. For your consulting positioning, this is validation that the urgency of AI strategy is real and that the window for organisations to lead rather than react is narrowing.

Two longevity items from credible sources today.

Nature Medicine has published a commentary arguing that the entire trajectory of obesity drug development needs to be reframed. The field has been obsessed with maximising weight loss — who can produce the biggest number on the scale — but the commentary makes the case that tolerability, long-term adherence, and medication persistence are the variables that actually determine patient outcomes. Two recent trials are cited as early examples of this reorientation. The practical implication: next-generation GLP-1 successors may be designed for sustained, comfortable use rather than maximum acute effect, which changes the risk-benefit calculus significantly for anyone thinking about these medications for long-term cardiometabolic management.

And from STAT News, which is on the allowlist: the FDA has cleared a new AI tool called EchoNext, built by Pathway Labs, that can screen for structural heart disease using a standard EKG. This is significant because structural cardiac conditions — things like hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, valve abnormalities, and early-stage heart failure — are chronically underdiagnosed in primary care settings because they typically require an echocardiogram, which is more expensive and less routinely ordered. If EchoNext can flag those conditions from an EKG that's already being done for other reasons, it could meaningfully improve early detection rates. Worth knowing about for yourself and your family's preventive health conversations with physicians.

That's your Tuesday briefing, Midya. The through-line today is really about windows — the window at TRU and in Canadian higher ed where consulting value is most visible, the window in applied AI marketing where early movers are building structural advantages, and the window in your own portfolio decisions while macro signals are mixed. The best use of your time today might be a short, thoughtful note to someone at TRU, and a close watch on what comes out of Minister Diab's press conference this afternoon. Both are moves that cost almost nothing and could matter a great deal. Make it a strong Tuesday.
